Q2: How can coding capabilities transfer to cybersecurity and other professional fields?
A3: Cybersecurity requires understanding code, identifying anomalies, calling tools to verify them, constructing multi-stage attack and defense processes, and adjusting plans based on environmental feedback. Its underlying capabilities are therefore highly aligned with those required by a complex coding Agent. On CyberGym, GLM-5.2 scored approximately 77.2, while GLM-5.3 improved to 84.5. On ExploitBench, the score increased from approximately 24.4 to 54.4. The closer a task is to a complete exploitation chain, and the more it requires long-horizon planning, the more pronounced the improvement. Since GLM-5.2, we have worked with multiple domestic security teams on real codebases and identified approximately 2,436 vulnerabilities after expert screening and deduplication. More than 1,000 of these were high-risk vulnerabilities, spanning 269 projects. The next step is to continue transferring the long-horizon planning, tool-use, and error-recovery capabilities trained through coding into high-value professional work such as data analysis, complex automation, legal services, and finance.
Q3: What criteria does Zhipu use when selecting Cowork scenarios?
A4: Cowork is not simply everyday office assistance. It means undertaking or replacing real, complex workflows in professional fields. There are three criteria for selecting a scenario: the task must have a sufficiently high intellectual threshold; the result must be capable of effective verification; and completing the task must create sufficiently high economic value. Cybersecurity is currently the clearest validated direction. Legal services, finance, data analysis, and other fields are also being explored, but their commercialization timelines will differ because their reliability thresholds and verification mechanisms are different. If each generation of models can complete longer, more complete, and more professional work, coding will become a meta-ability, and the boundary of high-value tasks the company can serve will continue to expand.
Q4: What is the current progress of compute expansion, and what is the structure of your compute resources?
A5: Since the beginning of the year, compute capacity has continued to expand at a healthy pace, with increased investment in both training and inference. Sources of compute include self-owned clusters, rented compute capacity, and purchased compute services. Uses cover pre-training, mid-training, post-training, and production inference. Different chip generations and architectures create a diverse and heterogeneous environment. Training efficiency and inference throughput vary substantially, so a simple count of accelerator cards can no longer accurately reflect compute supply or infrastructure capability. Internally, we focus more on effective compute: compute that has been installed, can be stably scheduled, can operate continuously over the long term, and can ultimately be converted into model-training progress or billable tokens. The core measure of a large-model company’s compute capability is not how many cards it owns, but how quickly those resources can support model iteration and how much commercial token supply they can provide.
Q5: At what scale are domestic chips being used in Zhipu’s inference business, and how are they performing?
A6: As of the first half of the year, we had achieved large-scale, low-cost inference on approximately 100,000 domestic accelerator cards. Our inference supply will not rely on a single channel of either imported or domestic cards as the sole path. When GLM-5.3 Flash was launched anonymously, the back end used domestic-chip clusters across the board to provide the service. In approximately six days, those clusters handled around 60 trillion tokens of usage and maintained strong service performance under historically high traffic on platforms such as OpenRouter and OpenCode. The ability of domestic accelerators and inference cards to run the workload has already been validated. The next stage will focus on economics: how to increase the effective-token output per unit of hardware under constraints such as memory capacity, bandwidth, and long-context workloads.
Q6: How much has infrastructure optimization improved inference efficiency on domestic chips?
A7: The company began executing an “all in Infra” strategy six months ago and rebuilt the inference engine and service stack for GLM-5.3. The optimization covered encode/decode, separation of prefill and decode, quantization, layer splitting, caching, communications, and other areas. On the same domestic hardware and with the same compute resources, overall end-to-end service performance improved by approximately three times compared with the initial baseline. Under limited and complex compute supply, improving efficiency through model-infrastructure co-optimization is more fundamental than merely expanding the sources of hardware. The main challenge in the next stage is to convert each unit of physical compute into more intelligence, more effective tokens, and greater commercial value.
Q7: What structural issues does training-side compute face, and how will they improve in the future?
A8: Training frontier models requires not only a large quantity of compute, but also the stability, network communications, software stack, and long-duration operating capability of large-scale homogeneous clusters. At present, China still relies mainly on heterogeneous compute. Advanced domestic accelerator cards have not yet fully entered large-scale volume production, creating a certain structural mismatch. Over roughly the next three to six months, advanced domestic chip manufacturers may begin ramping up volume, and the heterogeneous parallel-computing environment is expected to improve materially. Training of the base model is already progressing. Compute allocation will prioritize critical training windows, and we will not shift all resources to inference merely because inference demand is growing rapidly.
Q8: Does the model layer face a risk of commoditization, and how is Zhipu building pricing power?
A9: A single-point SOTA result cannot create long-term pricing power. Performance on public benchmarks and short tasks will gradually converge. However, long-duration, executable, and verifiable real-world tasks amplify the differences among models. Over approximately the past eleven months, GLM’s Intelligence Index on Artificial Analysis rose from 32 to 60, while the flagship model’s cost per task remained at around US$0.20. GLM-5.3 Flash reduced this further to approximately US$0.045. Pricing power depends on what a token can accomplish. One million tokens used for casual conversation create very different value for a customer from one million tokens used to complete an engineering project or repair a vulnerability in a production system. As models move from Coding toward Agent and Cowork, customers will gradually shift from buying tokens to buying task outcomes. Once a model enters a customer’s codebase, toolchain, internal data, and workflows, the customer will accumulate prompts, Agent workflows, permission systems, evaluation standards, and engineering integrations around it. Switching costs will then involve far more than the API price alone.
Q9: Have commercial data already demonstrated that capability improvements can support price increases?
A10: In the first half of the year, the average API selling price increased by approximately 101%, while token usage also rose substantially. Measured by revenue, the top ten customers’ average daily usage increased by approximately 98 times compared with the beginning of the year. The fact that prices rose while core customers deepened their usage shows that customers are not using the models only because they are inexpensive. As capabilities improve, customers are willing to entrust more real tasks to the models and pay for stronger capabilities. The industry may eventually develop two pricing curves. At a given level of intelligence, prices will continue to decline. Frontier models that open new task boundaries and materially improve success rates may still command a premium or even raise prices further.
Q10: What stage is the overseas business currently in, and how will it expand?
A11: The company has developed overseas business at a certain scale since 2025. Early efforts focused mainly on local deployment and sovereign large-model projects. Malaysia’s Matrix large-model project was one of the earlier overseas initiatives. As the business format has changed, the overseas focus has shifted toward the open platform and APIs. GLM-5.3 represents higher-level intelligence, while GLM-5.3 Flash represents accessibility and high cost-performance. They occupy distinct ecosystem positions in the high-value-task layer and the broadly accessible layer. We are actively advancing cooperation with overseas CSP platforms. In the future, we will expand overseas markets through open-source models, local hosting, revenue-sharing, and other approaches. Further progress may be disclosed over the next one to two months. Chinese models still lag the very top overseas models, but the Pareto-optimal combination of overall capability and cost can become an important entry point for overseas competition.
Q11: What are the most important improvement directions for the next generation of GLM models?
A12: Scaling has never stopped; the objective remains to raise the intelligence frontier. We previously invested in multimodal, image-generation, and video-generation research, but those directions provided limited help in raising the upper bound of intelligence. We therefore shifted our focus toward text, as well as model forms in which text and multimodal capabilities reinforce one another. Model capability is moving from answering knowledge questions to completing tasks. The research focus is accordingly shifting from basic question answering toward Coding and Cowork. The next-generation model will continue in this direction. The base model will continue to expand so that it can better store and represent knowledge. At the same time, we will increase reasoning depth through approaches such as smaller active parameter counts combined with loops, avoiding a situation in which multi-trillion-parameter models become too slow and expensive because their active parameter count is excessively large. In addition to scaling the base model, post-training will be significantly strengthened. We will use both technical and engineering methods to narrow the gap created by China’s compute constraints relative to overseas companies such as OpenAI and Anthropic.
Q12: Why were data environments and post-training important sources of GLM-5.3’s improvement?
A13: Around the time ChatGPT was released in 2022, Zhipu had already established a data-annotation team of several hundred people and had been investing over the long term in data and training-environment development. One important reason GLM-5.3 improved substantially over GLM-5.2 is that the scale of its data environments expanded by several dozen times. We will continue scaling data and environments in the future. The amount of new text data appearing on the internet is gradually declining, while the share of synthetic data is rising. Therefore, in addition to increasing base-model parameters, it is even more important to build verifiable data environments and real task environments so that models can continue receiving effective feedback during post-training.
Q13: What is the Fully Self-Training envisioned for GLM-6.0?
A14: Fully Self-Training corresponds to a model with self-evolution capabilities and is also commonly referred to overseas as RSI. The objective is for the model to conduct more of its own training and self-evolution across pre-training, mid-training, and post-training. The greatest challenge is not simply making the model larger or continuing to train it. It is enabling the model to assess itself, know when to stop, and autonomously correct itself when it makes an error. Fully Self-Training will become an important direction for future model research. Ethics and social governance will also be incorporated into the model-evolution process.
Q14: Why are you currently relatively restrained in parameter scale?
A15: The choice of model scale must take into account resources, model objectives, and when users will actually be able to use the model. The amount of training data available domestically is typically around 30–50 trillion tokens. At that data scale, blindly training an especially large model according to scaling laws may not produce sufficiently high marginal returns. Domestic compute is limited, while the potential of mid-training and post-training has not yet been fully released. Simply increasing parameters is therefore not the most important investment direction at present. The 745-billion-parameter base model underlying GLM-5.3 completed training at the beginning of the year and was planned from the outset for reuse over more than half a year. On the same base, we successively advanced GLM-5.1, 5.2, and 5.3, along with the corresponding SFT, mid-training, and post-training environment development. The basic approach is to extract the maximum capability from each base model while optimizing inference costs to a level that users can genuinely afford at scale, rather than merely pursuing a large model that cannot be deployed.
Q15: How are you planning the next-generation base model and its inference deployment?
A16: The next large base model is already moving forward, although its specific parameter count has not yet been disclosed. Mid-training and post-training will also be systematically planned on top of the new base. Inference research and engineering have already begun in advance. The goal is for the next-generation model to support full-scale user demand from the first day of release, rather than requiring a long period of engineering adaptation after launch.
